interpretation: Canonical concepts, their course occurrences and typed mathematical relations across courses. Curricular and mathematical structure only: nothing here records, implies or replaces evidence of the student's understanding, and a concept without evidence is untested, not weak.

concept_kinds.definition: A defined object, property or structure (sigma-algebra, holomorphic function, ideal, Fock space).
concept_kinds.theorem: A named or numbered proved statement (dominated convergence, Cauchy's theorem, Lagrange's theorem).
concept_kinds.inequality: A quantitative bound used as a tool (Hölder, Cauchy estimates, Chebyshev).
concept_kinds.technique: A method or recurring argument (truncation, keyhole contour, Wick contraction).
concept_kinds.construction: A procedure that produces an object (product measure, quotient ring, canonical quantization).
concept_kinds.example: A specific example or counterexample that recurs in the course.
concept_kinds.equation: A named equation of motion or identity (Klein-Gordon equation, Euler-Lagrange equations).
concept_kinds.principle: A physical postulate or principle taken as input rather than proved (causality, unitarity, locality).
concept_kinds.model: A specific theory, Lagrangian or system studied as an object (phi^4 theory, the free complex scalar).

relation_classes.dependency: One concept is needed for, used in proving, or applied to obtain the other. Defines the dependency depth and must be acyclic across all courses.
relation_classes.logical: A precise logical relation between statements or definitions (special case, implication, equivalence, counterexample). Not a dependency.
relation_classes.structural: Both concern the same precisely identifiable mathematical object or structure, without a dependency between them.

prerequisite.meaning: Source is needed to state or understand the target.
prerequisite.reads_as: SOURCE is a prerequisite of TARGET

used_in_proof.meaning: Source is a step or tool in a standard proof of the target.
used_in_proof.reads_as: SOURCE is used in a standard proof of TARGET
used_in_proof.target_note: The target should be a provable claim. If the target is a definition, the relation is about the claim embedded in it (for example that L^p is normed); prefer prerequisite unless the proof is the point.

generalizes.meaning: Source is a more general statement; the target is a special case.
generalizes.reads_as: SOURCE generalizes TARGET (TARGET is a special case of SOURCE)

equivalent_formulation.meaning: The two express the same mathematical content in different terms.
equivalent_formulation.reads_as: SOURCE and TARGET are equivalent formulations
equivalent_formulation.example: two characterizations of the same property
equivalent_formulation.cross_course_rule: Across courses an equivalence must state, in `conditions`, the exact identification and hypotheses under which it holds. Two ids that name the same concept are a duplicate identity, not an equivalence: merge them with a registry redirect instead.

application.meaning: Target is an application or consequence obtained by applying the source.
application.reads_as: TARGET is obtained by applying SOURCE

shares_structure.meaning: Both concern the same mathematical object or structure, without a dependency.
shares_structure.reads_as: SOURCE and TARGET concern the same precisely identifiable structure
shares_structure.example: two results about the same object proved independently
shares_structure.cross_course_rule: Name the shared structure in `conditions`. A resemblance with no precisely identifiable common object is an association of kind analogy, not shares_structure.

counterexample.meaning: Source is an example showing that a hypothesis of, or a converse to, the target fails.
counterexample.reads_as: SOURCE is a counterexample showing a hypothesis of (or the converse of) TARGET is needed

implies.meaning: Whenever the source holds, the target holds (for example, one mode of convergence implies another).

association_kinds.analogy: A heuristic resemblance between concepts with no precise common structure or dependency (for example a probabilistic and a physical notion that behave alike). Never a relation; never moves the structure channel.
association_kinds.thematic: The concepts belong to the same theme or recur together in a course without a mathematical link. Never moves the structure channel.
association_kinds.homonym: Same or similar name, different mathematics (characteristic function of a random variable vs. indicator function). Records that the two must NOT be merged.

statuses.proposed: Proposed by a builder agent or extracted from a source; not yet reviewed.
statuses.agent_reviewed: Confirmed (possibly after correction) by an independent reviewer agent that did not propose it and read the sources. Never displayed or counted as human-verified.
statuses.verified: Human-verified: a named person confirmed it. Only `--apply-review --by <person>` sets it.
statuses.rejected: Rejected by a reviewer agent or a person. Kept for the audit trail; excluded from every channel and export.

occurrence_roles.core: Taught as a topic of this course (stated, defined or proved in lectures or assigned reading).
occurrence_roles.supporting: Used in this course as a tool, but taught elsewhere or assumed.
occurrence_roles.recalled: Mentioned or recalled for context only.

anchor_kinds.section: A textbook or notes section in the course's reading order: {source, ref, printed_page?, pdf_page?}. The only anchor kind that sets reading-order position.
anchor_kinds.result: A numbered or named result: {source, ref, title?, printed_page?, pdf_page?}. Must resolve in the course's index for that source.
anchor_kinds.equation: A numbered equation: {source, ref}. Must resolve in the course's index for that source.
anchor_kinds.page: A page reference without a numbered item: {source, printed_page and/or pdf_page, note?}.
anchor_kinds.lecture: A lecture heading: {topic} where topic is a curriculum.json topic id; the date comes from the course scope file.
anchor_kinds.exercise: An assigned textbook exercise: {source, ref, assignment, problem}. Must match materials/assignments.json.
anchor_kinds.homework_problem: A problem written on an assignment sheet: {assignment, problem, parts?}. Must match materials/assignments.json.
anchor_kinds.syllabus: Syllabus coverage: {unit} where unit is a syllabus_units id in the course scope file.

cited.label: a course source cites it by number

named.label: a course source names it in the statement or proof

concepts.name: σ-algebra
concepts.summary: A collection F of subsets of Ω containing Ω and closed under complements and countable unions; the domain on which a measure is defined. Countable operations stay inside F, and unions can be disjointized.

concepts.name: Measure
concepts.summary: A map μ: F → [0,∞] with μ(∅)=0 that is countably additive on disjoint sets: μ(⋃A_n)=Σμ(A_n). The triple (Ω,F,μ) is a measure space; μ is finite, σ-finite, or atomless depending on its masses.

concepts.name: Probability space
concepts.summary: A measure space (Ω,F,P) with total mass P(Ω)=1. Events are sets in F and P assigns them probabilities; every statement about random variables is ultimately a statement about P on F.

concepts.name: Algebra of sets
concepts.summary: A collection closed under complements and finite unions, such as finite disjoint unions of intervals. A premeasure that is countably additive on an algebra is the input to Carathéodory extension.

concepts.name: Continuity of measure
concepts.summary: For increasing events A_n ↑ A, μ(A_n) ↑ μ(A); for decreasing A_n ↓ A with μ(A_1)<∞, μ(A_n) ↓ μ(A). The finite-mass caveat matters: A_n=[n,∞) under Lebesgue measure.

concepts.name: Non-measurable sets
aliases: why volume cannot be assigned to every set
concepts.summary: Using the axiom of choice, a translation-invariant, countably additive length cannot be defined on every subset of [0,1). This forces measures to live on a σ-algebra rather than the full power set.

concepts.name: Generated σ-algebra
concepts.summary: σ(A) is the intersection of all σ-algebras containing the class A: the smallest σ-algebra containing it. Proofs about σ(A) usually check a property on generators and show the good sets form a σ-algebra.

concepts.name: Borel σ-algebra
concepts.summary: The σ-algebra generated by the open sets of a topological space. On R it is generated by intervals (a,b] with rational endpoints, or by half-lines (-∞,x], a countable generating class.

concepts.name: π-system
concepts.summary: A nonempty class of sets closed under finite intersections, such as half-lines (-∞,x] or measurable rectangles. Two finite measures agreeing on a π-system agree on the σ-algebra it generates.

concepts.name: λ-system
concepts.summary: A class containing Ω, closed under proper differences B∖A for A⊆B, and under increasing unions. A class that is both a π-system and a λ-system is a σ-algebra.

concepts.name: π–λ theorem
concepts.summary: If P is a π-system contained in a λ-system L, then σ(P) ⊆ L. It turns a property verified on an intersection-closed generating class into a property of the whole generated σ-algebra.

concepts.name: Uniqueness of measures
concepts.summary: Two measures that agree on a π-system P and are σ-finite on P agree on σ(P). In particular a probability law on R is determined by its values on half-lines, that is, by its distribution function.

concepts.name: Outer measure
concepts.summary: μ*(E)=inf Σμ_0(A_n) over countable covers of E by algebra sets; countably subadditive on all subsets. The Carathéodory-measurable sets, those splitting every set additively, form a σ-algebra.

concepts.name: Carathéodory extension theorem
concepts.summary: A countably additive premeasure μ_0 on an algebra A extends to a measure on σ(A); the extension is built from the outer measure, and it is unique when μ_0 is σ-finite.

concepts.name: Lebesgue measure
concepts.summary: The unique measure on the Borel sets of R assigning each interval its length b−a, obtained by extending interval length from the algebra of finite disjoint interval unions.

concepts.name: Completion of a measure
concepts.summary: Adding all subsets of null sets to F and extending μ yields a complete measure space; the Lebesgue σ-algebra is the completion of the Borel σ-algebra.

concepts.name: Measurable function / random variable
concepts.summary: A map X: (Ω,F) → (S,S) with X^{-1}(B) ∈ F for every B in S. It suffices to check inverse images of a generating class, for example {X ≤ x} for real X.

concepts.name: σ-algebra generated by a random variable
concepts.summary: σ(X) = {X^{-1}(B): B Borel}, the smallest σ-algebra making X measurable. It models the information revealed by observing X; Y is σ(X)-measurable exactly when Y is a Borel function of X.

concepts.name: Indicators and simple functions
concepts.summary: Finite linear combinations Σ c_k 1_{A_k} of indicators of measurable sets. Integrals, independence and measurability are defined or checked first on simple functions.

concepts.name: Simple-function approximation
aliases: measurable functions are limits of simple functions
concepts.summary: Every nonnegative measurable X is the increasing pointwise limit of simple functions X_n = min(n, 2^{-n}⌊2^n X⌋). This underpins the definition of the integral and the standard machine.

concepts.name: Functional monotone class theorem
concepts.summary: A vector space of bounded functions containing constants and indicators of a π-system, closed under bounded increasing limits, contains all bounded σ(P)-measurable functions. A function-level analogue of π–λ.

concepts.name: Closure properties of measurable functions
aliases: sums, products, compositions, sup, inf, limsup of measurable functions
concepts.summary: Continuous and monotone maps are Borel; compositions, sums, products, countable sup, inf, limsup and liminf of measurable functions are measurable, so pointwise limits of random variables are random variables.

concepts.name: Law of a random variable
concepts.summary: The probability measure P_X(B)=P(X∈B) on the target space, the pushforward of P under X. Many results depend on X only through its law.

concepts.name: Distribution function (CDF)
concepts.summary: F_X(x)=P(X≤x): nondecreasing, right-continuous, with limits 0 at −∞ and 1 at +∞. Jumps of F are atoms of the law; continuous mass produces no jump.

concepts.name: CDF characterization theorem
concepts.summary: Any nondecreasing right-continuous F with limits 0 and 1 is the distribution function of a unique probability measure on R, constructed by extension from F(b)−F(a) on intervals or via a quantile transform.

concepts.name: Equality in law versus almost surely
concepts.summary: X and Y are equal in law when P_X=P_Y, possibly on different probability spaces; X=Y almost surely is much stronger, requiring the same space and P(X≠Y)=0.

concepts.name: Support and atoms of a law
concepts.summary: The support is the smallest closed set of full measure; an atom is a point x with P(X=x)>0, seen as a jump of the CDF. Positive mass on an interval need not create any atom.

concepts.name: Lebesgue integral
aliases: integral with respect to a measure
concepts.summary: Defined for simple functions by Σ c_k μ(A_k), for nonnegative f as the supremum over simple functions below f, and for signed f as ∫f⁺−∫f⁻ when not both are infinite.

concepts.name: Expectation
concepts.summary: E[X]=∫ X dP, the Lebesgue integral of a random variable with respect to the probability measure; linear, monotone, and defined in [−∞,∞] when E X⁺ or E X⁻ is finite.

concepts.name: Additivity of the integral
concepts.summary: E[aX+bY]=aE[X]+bE[Y] for integrable X,Y, and E[Σ X_n]=Σ E[X_n] for nonnegative X_n; proved by passing from simple functions to monotone limits.

concepts.name: Standard machine
concepts.summary: Prove an integral identity for indicators, extend by linearity to simple functions, by monotone convergence to nonnegative functions, and by splitting f=f⁺−f⁻ to integrable functions.

concepts.name: Monotone convergence theorem
concepts.summary: If 0 ≤ X_n ↑ X almost surely then E[X_n] ↑ E[X]. Limits and integrals may be exchanged for increasing nonnegative sequences, with no integrability assumption.

concepts.name: Markov inequality
concepts.summary: For nonnegative X and a>0, P(X≥a) ≤ E[X]/a; more generally P(X≥a) ≤ E[f(X)]/f(a) for nondecreasing f ≥ 0. A zero integral of a nonnegative function forces it to vanish almost everywhere.

concepts.name: Chebyshev inequality
concepts.summary: Markov's inequality applied to (X−EX)²: P(|X−EX|≥t) ≤ Var(X)/t². The workhorse bound behind L² weak laws.

concepts.name: Chernoff bound
concepts.summary: Markov's inequality applied to e^{θX}: P(X≥a) ≤ e^{−θa}E[e^{θX}], optimized over θ>0; gives exponentially small tail probabilities when the moment generating function is finite.

concepts.name: Jensen inequality
concepts.summary: For convex φ and integrable X, φ(E[X]) ≤ E[φ(X)]; proved from a supporting line (hyperplane) at E[X]. Concave functions reverse the inequality, as in E log X ≤ log E X.

concepts.name: Hölder inequality
concepts.summary: For conjugate exponents 1/p+1/q=1, E|XY| ≤ ‖X‖_p‖Y‖_q, derived from Young's inequality ab ≤ a^p/p + b^q/q; equality needs |X|^p and |Y|^q proportional.

concepts.name: Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
concepts.summary: The case p=q=2 of Hölder: |E[XY]| ≤ (E[X²]E[Y²])^{1/2}; it bounds covariances and correlations and is the inner-product inequality of L².

concepts.name: Minkowski inequality
concepts.summary: ‖X+Y‖_p ≤ ‖X‖_p+‖Y‖_p for 1 ≤ p ≤ ∞, the triangle inequality making ‖·‖_p a seminorm; proved with Hölder applied to |X+Y|^{p−1}.

concepts.name: Lp spaces
concepts.summary: The random variables with E|X|^p<∞, modulo almost-sure equality, normed by ‖X‖_p=(E|X|^p)^{1/p}; quotienting turns the seminorm into a norm. Simple functions are dense for p<∞.

concepts.name: Essential supremum and L∞
concepts.summary: ‖X‖_∞ = inf{c: P(|X|>c)=0}, the smallest almost-sure bound; ‖X‖_p → ‖X‖_∞ as p→∞ on a probability space.

concepts.name: Nesting of Lp spaces
concepts.summary: On a probability space p ↦ ‖X‖_p is nondecreasing, so L^q ⊆ L^p for p ≤ q; it follows from Jensen with the convex map t ↦ t^{q/p}. Fails for infinite measures such as Lebesgue measure on R.

concepts.name: Almost sure convergence
aliases: pointwise convergence off a null set
concepts.summary: X_n → X a.s. when P({ω: X_n(ω) → X(ω)})=1; equivalently, for every ε>0, P(|X_n−X|>ε infinitely often)=0, which is a limsup-event (tail-type) statement.

concepts.name: Convergence in probability
concepts.summary: X_n → X in probability when P(|X_n−X|>ε) → 0 for every ε>0. Implied by a.s. and by Lp convergence; it implies a.s. convergence along a subsequence.

concepts.name: Convergence in Lp
concepts.summary: X_n → X in L^p when E|X_n−X|^p → 0. Markov's inequality shows it implies convergence in probability; the converse needs uniform integrability.

concepts.name: Convergence-mode counterexamples
concepts.summary: Indicators of intervals sweeping repeatedly across [0,1] converge in probability and in L^p but not almost surely; spikes n·1_{(0,1/n)} converge almost surely but not in L^1. They separate the convergence modes.

concepts.name: Fatou's lemma
concepts.summary: For nonnegative X_n, E[liminf X_n] ≤ liminf E[X_n]; proved by applying monotone convergence to the lower envelopes inf_{k≥n} X_k.

concepts.name: Dominated convergence theorem
concepts.summary: If X_n → X almost surely (or in probability) and |X_n| ≤ Y with E[Y]<∞, then E[X_n] → E[X] and E|X_n−X| → 0; proved by applying Fatou to Y±X_n.

concepts.name: Bounded convergence theorem
concepts.summary: If X_n → X almost surely and |X_n| ≤ K for a non-random constant K, then X is integrable and E|X_n − X| → 0; the case of dominated convergence with a constant dominating variable. Convergence in probability suffices, via uniform integrability.

concepts.name: Scheffé's lemma
aliases: densities converging pointwise converge in L1
concepts.summary: If nonnegative f_n → f almost everywhere and ∫f_n → ∫f < ∞, then ∫|f_n−f| → 0; for probability densities pointwise convergence gives total-variation convergence of the laws.

concepts.name: Uniform integrability
concepts.summary: A family {X_α} is uniformly integrable when sup_α E[|X_α|; |X_α|>M] → 0 as M→∞, equivalently bounded in L^1 with uniformly small integrals over small events. Domination by one integrable variable and bounded L^p norms (p>1) are sufficient conditions.

concepts.name: Vitali convergence theorem
aliases: UI plus convergence in probability gives L1 convergence
concepts.summary: X_n → X in L^1 if and only if X_n → X in probability and {X_n} is uniformly integrable; it sharpens dominated convergence into a characterization.

concepts.name: Density-weighted measure
concepts.summary: For measurable f ≥ 0, ν(A)=∫_A f dμ defines a measure, and ∫g dν = ∫ g f dμ by the standard machine. Probability densities are the case μ = Lebesgue measure and ∫f=1.

concepts.name: Absolute continuity and Radon–Nikodym
concepts.summary: If ν ≪ μ (μ-null sets are ν-null) and μ is σ-finite, then ν has a density dν/dμ. A Dirac mass is not absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure and so has no density.

concepts.name: Probability density
aliases: density of a law with respect to Lebesgue measure
concepts.summary: A nonnegative f with ∫f=1 such that P(X∈B)=∫_B f(x)dx; then E g(X)=∫ g(x) f(x) dx. Exists exactly when the law is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure.

concepts.name: Change of variables formula
concepts.summary: E[g(X)] = ∫ g(x) P_X(dx): expectations of functions of X can be computed on the target space using only the law of X; proved by the standard machine from indicators.

concepts.name: Independence
concepts.summary: σ-algebras F_1,…,F_n are independent when P(A_1∩…∩A_n)=ΠP(A_i) for all A_i∈F_i; random variables are independent when their generated σ-algebras are. Infinite families require every finite subfamily.

concepts.name: Pairwise versus mutual independence
aliases: three fair bits with a parity constraint
concepts.summary: Two fair bits and their XOR are pairwise independent but not mutually independent: mutual independence must test every finite subfamily, not only pairs.

concepts.name: Independence from generating π-systems
concepts.summary: If π-systems P_i are independent then σ(P_i) are independent; so independence of real random variables follows from factorization of P(X_1≤x_1,…,X_n≤x_n), and disjoint groups of independent variables are independent.

concepts.name: Tail σ-algebra
concepts.summary: T = ⋂_n σ(X_n,X_{n+1},…), the events unchanged by altering finitely many coordinates, such as {Σ X_n converges} or {limsup X_n > c}.

concepts.name: Kolmogorov 0–1 law
concepts.summary: For independent X_1,X_2,…, every tail event has probability 0 or 1, because the tail σ-algebra is independent of itself; tail random variables are almost surely constant.

concepts.name: Product σ-algebra
concepts.summary: The σ-algebra on Ω_1×Ω_2 (or an infinite product) generated by measurable rectangles A_1×A_2, equivalently the smallest one making coordinate projections measurable. On R^n it equals the Borel σ-algebra.

concepts.name: Product measure
concepts.summary: There is a unique measure on the product σ-algebra with μ(A_1×A_2)=μ_1(A_1)μ_2(A_2) for σ-finite factors; countable additivity is checked on the algebra of finite disjoint rectangle unions by slicing.

concepts.name: Independence as a product law
aliases: joint law equals product of marginals
concepts.summary: Random variables are independent if and only if their joint law is the product of their marginal laws, which links probabilistic independence to the product-measure construction.

concepts.name: Kolmogorov extension theorem
aliases: existence of a process on R^N
concepts.summary: A consistent family of finite-dimensional laws on R^n, n=1,2,…, comes from a unique probability measure on the infinite product (R^N, cylinder σ-algebra); in particular infinite i.i.d. sequences exist.

concepts.name: Existence of independent sequences
aliases: constructing independent coordinates with prescribed laws
concepts.summary: Given laws μ_1, μ_2, …, there is a probability space carrying independent X_i with X_i ~ μ_i, built as coordinates of a product space (or from binary digits of one uniform variable).

concepts.name: Fubini–Tonelli theorem
concepts.summary: For f ≥ 0 measurable on a σ-finite product, ∫ f d(μ_1⊗μ_2) equals both iterated integrals (Tonelli); for f integrable the same holds with finite values (Fubini). Proved by the monotone class method from rectangles.

concepts.name: Tail-integral formula for expectations
concepts.summary: For X ≥ 0, E[X] = ∫_0^∞ P(X>t) dt and E[X^p] = ∫_0^∞ p t^{p−1} P(X>t) dt, obtained by writing X = ∫_0^∞ 1_{t<X} dt and applying Tonelli.

concepts.name: Convolution of laws
aliases: law of a sum of independent variables
concepts.summary: If X and Y are independent, the law of X+Y is μ_X * μ_Y(B)=∫ μ_X(B−y) μ_Y(dy), with density ∫ f_X(z−y) f_Y(y) dy when densities exist; computed via Fubini on the product law.

concepts.name: Variance and covariance of sums
concepts.summary: Var(Σ X_k) = Σ Var(X_k) + 2Σ_{j<k} Cov(X_j,X_k); for uncorrelated variables the cross terms vanish, and decay of covariances controls the variance of averages.

concepts.name: L² weak law of large numbers
concepts.summary: If X_k are uncorrelated with bounded variances, S_n/n − E[S_n]/n → 0 in L² and hence in probability, because Var(S_n/n) ≤ C/n.

concepts.name: Truncation
concepts.summary: Replace X_k by X_k 1_{|X_k| ≤ b_n} so second moments exist, control the variance of the truncated sum, and show the discarded part is negligible; extends weak laws to variables with only a first moment.

concepts.name: Weak law of large numbers
aliases: convergence of sample means in probability
concepts.summary: For i.i.d. integrable X_k, S_n/n → E[X_1] in probability; proved by truncation plus a second-moment bound even without finite variance.

concepts.name: Limsup events (infinitely often)
concepts.summary: limsup A_n = ⋂_n ⋃_{k≥n} A_k is the event that infinitely many A_n occur; liminf A_n is the event that all but finitely many occur. Almost sure convergence is phrased through such events.

concepts.name: First Borel–Cantelli lemma
concepts.summary: If Σ P(A_n) < ∞ then P(A_n infinitely often) = 0, with no independence assumption; proved from E[Σ 1_{A_n}] < ∞ or by continuity of measure.

concepts.name: Second Borel–Cantelli lemma
aliases: independent events with divergent sum occur infinitely often
concepts.summary: If the A_n are independent and Σ P(A_n) = ∞ then P(A_n infinitely often) = 1; independence (or a pairwise substitute) is essential.

concepts.name: Second-moment method
concepts.summary: Lower-bounds P(Z>0) ≥ (E Z)²/E[Z²] for counts Z=Σ1_{A_k}; the Kochen–Stone lemma gives P(A_n i.o.) ≥ limsup (Σ P(A_k))²/Σ_{j,k} P(A_j∩A_k) without full independence.

concepts.name: Subsequence method
concepts.summary: Prove almost sure convergence along a sparse subsequence n_k (often geometric) with summable error probabilities via Borel–Cantelli, then control fluctuations between n_k and n_{k+1} using monotonicity.

concepts.name: A.s. convergence along a subsequence
aliases: convergence in probability implies a.s. convergence along a subsequence
concepts.summary: If X_n → X in probability, there is a subsequence with X_{n_k} → X almost surely: choose n_k with P(|X_{n_k}−X|>2^{-k}) ≤ 2^{-k} and apply the first Borel–Cantelli lemma.

concepts.name: Strong law of large numbers
concepts.summary: For i.i.d. X_k with E|X_1| < ∞, S_n/n → E[X_1] almost surely; with E[X_1⁺]=∞ and E[X_1⁻]<∞ the averages tend to +∞. Proved by truncation, a variance bound on a subsequence, and Borel–Cantelli.

concepts.name: Kolmogorov maximal inequality
concepts.summary: For independent mean-zero square-integrable X_k, P(max_{k≤n}|S_k| ≥ t) ≤ Var(S_n)/t²: Chebyshev's bound holds for the whole path of partial sums, not just its endpoint.

concepts.name: Convergence of random series
concepts.summary: For independent X_n, Σ Var(X_n) < ∞ with mean-zero terms implies Σ X_n converges almost surely; the three-series theorem characterizes almost sure convergence using truncation. By the 0–1 law the probability of convergence is 0 or 1.

concepts.name: Normal distribution
concepts.summary: The law with density (2πσ²)^{-1/2} exp(−(x−μ)²/(2σ²)) and characteristic function exp(iμt − σ²t²/2); stable under independent sums and the universal limit in the central limit theorem.

concepts.name: Central limit theorem
concepts.summary: For i.i.d. X_k with mean μ and finite variance σ², (S_n − nμ)/(σ√n) converges in distribution to a standard normal; the scaling √n is the size of typical fluctuations of the sum.

concepts.name: Lindeberg–Feller CLT
concepts.summary: For a triangular array of independent row entries with total variance 1, the Lindeberg condition Σ E[X_{n,k}²; |X_{n,k}|>ε] → 0 implies the row sums converge in distribution to N(0,1); Lyapunov's condition is a sufficient special case.

concepts.name: Convergence in distribution
concepts.summary: X_n ⇒ X when F_{X_n}(x) → F_X(x) at every continuity point x of F_X, equivalently E g(X_n) → E g(X) for bounded continuous g; it only concerns laws, so the X_n may live on different spaces.

concepts.name: Skorokhod representation
aliases: almost sure representation of weak convergence
concepts.summary: If X_n ⇒ X, there are Y_n =d X_n and Y =d X on one probability space with Y_n → Y almost surely, built from quantile functions of a single uniform variable; it lets a.s. tools prove distributional statements.

concepts.name: Slutsky's lemma
aliases: X_n ⇒ X and Y_n → c imply X_n + Y_n ⇒ X + c
concepts.summary: If X_n ⇒ X and Y_n → c in probability for a constant c, then X_n+Y_n ⇒ X+c and X_nY_n ⇒ cX; negligible perturbations do not change a distributional limit.

concepts.name: Weak convergence of measures
aliases: ∫ g dμ_n → ∫ g dμ for bounded continuous g
concepts.summary: Probability measures μ_n ⇒ μ when ∫g dμ_n → ∫g dμ for all bounded continuous g; the portmanteau theorem gives equivalent forms with open sets, closed sets, and μ-continuity sets.

concepts.name: Tightness and Helly selection
aliases: no escape of mass to infinity
concepts.summary: A family of laws is tight if for each ε some compact set carries mass at least 1−ε under all of them; Helly's selection theorem says every tight sequence on R has a weakly convergent subsequence.

concepts.name: Characteristic function
concepts.summary: φ_X(t) = E[e^{itX}], the Fourier transform of the law of X; it always exists, is uniformly continuous with |φ| ≤ 1, and turns convolution of independent laws into multiplication.

concepts.name: Characteristic functions and moments
concepts.summary: If E|X|^n < ∞ then φ_X is n times continuously differentiable with φ^{(k)}(0) = i^k E[X^k]; sharp bounds on the remainder of the Taylor expansion of e^{ix} control φ near 0.

concepts.name: Lévy inversion formula
aliases: the characteristic function determines the law
concepts.summary: μ((a,b)) + μ({a,b})/2 = lim_{T→∞} (2π)^{-1} ∫_{−T}^{T} (e^{−ita} − e^{−itb})/(it) φ(t) dt, so a law is determined by its characteristic function; integrable φ gives a continuous density.

concepts.name: Lévy continuity theorem
aliases: convergence of characteristic functions implies convergence in distribution
concepts.summary: X_n ⇒ X if and only if φ_{X_n}(t) → φ_X(t) for every t; if φ_{X_n} converges pointwise to a function continuous at 0, the laws are tight and converge to the law with that characteristic function.

concepts.name: Holomorphic function
concepts.summary: A complex-valued function on an open subset of the plane whose difference quotient has a limit at every point as the increment tends to 0 through all complex directions. This one condition forces infinite differentiability and local power-series expansions, unlike real differentiability.

concepts.name: Cauchy–Riemann equations
concepts.summary: Writing f = u + iv, complex differentiability at a point forces u_x = v_y and u_y = -v_x there; conversely, if u and v are continuously differentiable and satisfy these equations on an open set, f is holomorphic. They also take a polar form in r and θ.

concepts.name: Power series
aliases: series in powers of z - z0
concepts.summary: A series of the form sum a_n (z - z0)^n. It converges absolutely on an open disc about z0 and diverges outside the closed disc, so its region of convergence is governed by a single radius.

concepts.name: Complex exponential
concepts.summary: The entire function e^z defined by its everywhere-convergent power series; e^{x+iy} = e^x(cos y + i sin y), it is 2πi-periodic, its own derivative, and a homomorphism from the additive group of C onto the nonzero complex numbers under multiplication.

concepts.name: Cauchy–Hadamard formula
concepts.summary: The radius of convergence of sum a_n z^n equals 1 / limsup |a_n|^{1/n} (with 1/0 = ∞ and 1/∞ = 0): the series converges absolutely inside that radius and diverges outside it.

concepts.name: Termwise differentiation of power series
concepts.summary: A power series is holomorphic inside its disc of convergence, and its derivative is the series differentiated term by term, which has the same radius; iterating, power series are infinitely complex differentiable there.

concepts.name: Piecewise-smooth curve
concepts.summary: A continuous map from a closed interval into the plane made of finitely many continuously differentiable pieces with nonvanishing derivative; curves are taken up to orientation-preserving reparametrization, and closed and simple curves are distinguished.

concepts.name: Contour integral
concepts.summary: The integral of a continuous complex function along a piecewise-smooth curve, defined by pulling back through a parametrization: the integral of f(γ(t))γ'(t) dt. It is independent of orientation-preserving reparametrization and changes sign when the orientation is reversed.

concepts.name: Primitive of a complex function
concepts.summary: A holomorphic function F on an open set whose complex derivative equals a given function f there. On a connected open set, f has a primitive exactly when its integrals over all closed curves vanish, and primitives differ by constants.

concepts.name: Fundamental theorem for contour integrals
concepts.summary: If a continuous function has a primitive F on an open set, its integral along any curve there equals F at the endpoint minus F at the starting point; in particular its integral over every closed curve vanishes.

concepts.name: Length–maximum estimate
concepts.summary: The modulus of a contour integral is at most the supremum of |f| on the curve times the curve's length. It is the basic tool for showing that integrals over large or small arcs tend to zero.

concepts.name: Goursat's theorem
concepts.summary: The integral of a holomorphic function over the boundary of any triangle that lies, together with its interior, in the domain is zero. The proof subdivides the triangle repeatedly and uses only complex differentiability, with no continuity assumption on the derivative.

concepts.name: Existence of primitives on discs
concepts.summary: A holomorphic function on an open disc (more generally on a star-shaped open set) has a primitive there, obtained by integrating along polygonal paths from the centre and using Goursat's theorem to make the result path independent.

concepts.name: Cauchy's theorem
concepts.summary: The integral of a holomorphic function over a closed curve vanishes when the curve lies in a disc, and more generally in any simply connected open set (or when the curve is null-homotopic) inside the domain of holomorphy.

concepts.name: Cauchy integral formula
concepts.summary: A function holomorphic on a neighbourhood of a closed disc is recovered at interior points from its boundary values by integrating f(ζ)/(ζ − z) around the circle and dividing by 2πi; differentiating under the integral gives every derivative, so holomorphic functions are infinitely differentiable.

concepts.name: Cauchy inequalities
concepts.summary: For f holomorphic on a neighbourhood of a closed disc of radius R about z0, the n-th derivative at z0 is bounded in modulus by n! times the maximum of |f| on the boundary circle divided by R^n.

concepts.name: Holomorphic functions are analytic
concepts.summary: A holomorphic function equals its Taylor series on every disc whose closure lies in its domain; the series converges at least up to the nearest boundary point, and its coefficients are the derivatives at the centre divided by n!.

concepts.name: Entire function
aliases: function holomorphic on the whole plane
concepts.summary: A function holomorphic on all of C, such as polynomials, the exponential and the sine. Growth restrictions on entire functions translate into strong algebraic constraints, beginning with Liouville's theorem.

concepts.name: Liouville's theorem
concepts.summary: Every bounded entire function is constant. It follows by letting the radius tend to infinity in the Cauchy inequality for the first derivative.

concepts.name: Fundamental theorem of algebra
aliases: every polynomial has a complex root
concepts.summary: Every non-constant polynomial with complex coefficients has a root in C, hence factors completely into linear factors. One proof: if it had no root, its reciprocal would be a bounded entire function.

concepts.name: Order of a zero and local factorization
concepts.summary: If a holomorphic function on a connected open set vanishes at a point but not identically, it factors near that point as (z − z0)^n times a nonvanishing holomorphic function, for a unique positive integer n called the order or multiplicity of the zero.

concepts.name: Identity theorem
concepts.summary: If a holomorphic function on a connected open set vanishes on a set with a limit point in that set, it vanishes identically; hence two holomorphic functions agreeing on such a set agree everywhere, and the zeros of a nonzero holomorphic function are isolated.

concepts.name: Analytic continuation
concepts.summary: Extending a holomorphic function from a smaller connected open set to a larger one. Such an extension, if it exists, is unique by the identity theorem; some functions admit no continuation across any boundary point of their domain.

concepts.name: Local injectivity and nonvanishing derivative
concepts.summary: A holomorphic function is one-to-one near a point exactly when its derivative there is nonzero; then it has a holomorphic local inverse whose derivative is the reciprocal. In particular an injective holomorphic map has nowhere-vanishing derivative.

concepts.name: Morera's theorem
concepts.summary: A continuous function on an open disc whose integral over every triangle in the disc vanishes is holomorphic. It converts integral identities into holomorphy and is the usual way to prove that limits and reflections of holomorphic functions are holomorphic.

concepts.name: Locally uniform limits of holomorphic functions
concepts.summary: If holomorphic functions converge uniformly on every compact subset of an open set, the limit is holomorphic and the derivatives converge locally uniformly to its derivative.

concepts.name: Schwarz reflection principle
concepts.summary: A holomorphic function on a region in the upper half-plane that extends continuously and real-valued to a segment of the real axis extends holomorphically across the segment by f(conj z) conjugated; the gluing step is the symmetry principle, proved with Morera's theorem.

concepts.name: Isolated singularity
concepts.summary: A point where a function is holomorphic on a punctured neighbourhood but not necessarily at the point itself. It is removable, a pole of some order (where the function behaves like a negative power), or essential, distinguished by the limiting behaviour or by the principal part.

concepts.name: Laurent series
concepts.summary: An expansion sum over all integers n of a_n (z − z0)^n for a function holomorphic on an annulus, with coefficients given by contour integrals over a circle in the annulus. The negative-power part is the principal part, which classifies an isolated singularity.

concepts.name: Residue
concepts.summary: The coefficient of (z − z0)^{-1} in the Laurent expansion at an isolated singularity, equal to the integral over a small circle divided by 2πi. At a pole of order m it is computed by differentiating (z − z0)^m f m − 1 times; at a simple pole of g/h it is g/h'.

concepts.name: Residue theorem
concepts.summary: For a function holomorphic on a neighbourhood of a region bounded by a positively oriented simple closed contour, except at finitely many isolated singularities inside, the integral over the contour equals 2πi times the sum of the residues there.

concepts.name: Evaluating real integrals by contour integration
concepts.summary: Computing definite integrals over the real line or over angles by closing the path in the complex plane (semicircles, rectangles, sectors, keyholes), applying Cauchy's theorem or the residue theorem, and showing the added pieces vanish or are computable in the limit.

concepts.name: Indented contour
concepts.summary: A contour that detours around a singularity on the path of integration with a small arc; as the arc shrinks, a simple pole contributes a fixed fraction of 2πi times its residue (half for a semicircle), which produces principal-value integrals.

concepts.name: Cauchy principal value
concepts.summary: The symmetric limit that defines an integral through a singularity or over an infinite range, excising an interval of radius ε about the bad point (or truncating symmetrically) and letting ε tend to 0; it can exist when the improper integral does not.

concepts.name: Fresnel integrals
concepts.summary: The improper integrals of sin(x^2) and cos(x^2) over the positive axis, both equal to √(2π)/4. They are evaluated by integrating e^{-z^2} around the boundary of a sector of angle π/4 and comparing with the Gaussian integral.

concepts.name: Coefficient extraction from generating functions
concepts.summary: Recovering the coefficients of a power series, such as a combinatorial generating function, as contour integrals around the origin; deforming the contour and summing residues at the poles gives exact formulas and asymptotics, with the radius of convergence set by the nearest singularity.

concepts.name: Riemann's removable singularity theorem
concepts.summary: A function holomorphic on a punctured neighbourhood of a point and bounded near it extends holomorphically to the point; equivalently all negative Laurent coefficients vanish.

concepts.name: Casorati–Weierstrass theorem
concepts.summary: Near an essential singularity, a holomorphic function takes values arbitrarily close to every complex number: the image of every punctured neighbourhood is dense in the plane.

concepts.name: Meromorphic function
concepts.summary: A function holomorphic on an open set except at a discrete set of poles. Quotients of holomorphic functions are meromorphic after cancelling common zeros, and the meromorphic functions on the extended plane are exactly the rational functions.

concepts.name: Riemann sphere
concepts.summary: The plane with one point at infinity added, identified with the sphere by stereographic projection; charts z and 1/z describe behaviour at infinity, and Möbius maps act on it as bijections.

concepts.name: Argument principle
concepts.summary: For f meromorphic near a region bounded by a simple closed contour with no zeros or poles on it, the integral of f'/f over the contour divided by 2πi equals the number of zeros minus the number of poles inside, counted with multiplicity; it is the winding number of the image curve about 0.

concepts.name: Rouché's theorem
concepts.summary: A zero-counting comparison: when a holomorphic perturbation g is strictly smaller in modulus than f on the boundary of a closed disc (or a region with simple closed boundary), adding g leaves the multiplicity-weighted count of zeros of f inside unchanged.

concepts.name: Open mapping theorem
concepts.summary: A non-constant holomorphic function on a connected open set maps open sets to open sets: every value taken at a point is also taken at all nearby values, by a zero-counting argument.

concepts.name: Maximum modulus principle
concepts.summary: The modulus of a non-constant holomorphic function on a connected open set has no local maximum; on a bounded region with continuous extension to the closure, the maximum of |f| is attained on the boundary.

concepts.name: Homotopy of curves
concepts.summary: A continuous deformation of one curve into another inside a set, either keeping endpoints fixed or keeping closed curves closed throughout.

concepts.name: Homotopy invariance of contour integrals
concepts.summary: If f is holomorphic on an open set, its integrals along two curves that are homotopic in that set (fixed endpoints, or through closed curves) are equal; the proof covers the homotopy by small discs carrying local primitives.

concepts.name: Simply connected domain
concepts.summary: A connected open set in which every closed curve can be continuously contracted to a point without leaving the set. On such sets holomorphic functions have primitives, nonvanishing ones have logarithms, and harmonic functions have conjugates.

concepts.name: Branch of the complex logarithm
concepts.summary: On a simply connected open set avoiding 0 there is a holomorphic L with e^L = z, given by integrating 1/w from a base point; more generally a nowhere-zero holomorphic function on a simply connected set has a holomorphic logarithm, hence n-th roots. Branches differ by multiples of 2πi.

concepts.name: Branch cut
concepts.summary: A curve removed from the plane so that a multivalued expression such as log z, z^a or a square root has a single-valued holomorphic branch on what remains, for example the slit plane C minus (−∞, 0] for the principal logarithm.

concepts.name: Conformal map
concepts.summary: A holomorphic bijection between open sets; its inverse is automatically holomorphic and its derivative never vanishes, so it preserves angles. Two sets joined by one are conformally equivalent, and the conformal self-maps form the automorphism group.

concepts.name: Möbius transformation
concepts.summary: A map z ↦ (az + b)/(cz + d) with ad − bc ≠ 0, a bijection of the Riemann sphere taking circles and lines to circles and lines. Composition matches matrix multiplication, so the Möbius group is GL2(C) modulo nonzero scalars.

concepts.name: Cayley transform
concepts.summary: The Möbius map z ↦ (z − i)/(z + i), a conformal bijection from the upper half-plane onto the unit disc with inverse w ↦ i(1 + w)/(1 − w); it transports questions between the two models.

concepts.name: Schwarz lemma
concepts.summary: A holomorphic self-map f of the unit disc with f(0) = 0 satisfies |f(z)| ≤ |z| and |f'(0)| ≤ 1, with equality at one nonzero point or for the derivative only when f is a rotation.

concepts.name: Schwarz–Pick inequality
concepts.summary: A holomorphic self-map of the unit disc does not increase the pseudo-hyperbolic distance |(z − w)/(1 − conj(w) z)| between points; it is the Schwarz lemma made invariant under disc automorphisms.

concepts.name: Blaschke factor
concepts.summary: For a point α of the unit disc, the map z ↦ (α − z)/(1 − conj(α) z): a holomorphic bijection of the disc onto itself that swaps 0 and α, is its own inverse and has modulus 1 on the unit circle.

concepts.name: Automorphisms of the unit disc
concepts.summary: Every conformal self-map of the unit disc is a rotation composed with a Blaschke factor; those fixing 0 are the rotations. The group acts transitively, so the disc is the coset space of the group by the circle of rotations, and it is a matrix group of the SU(1,1) type modulo ±1.

concepts.name: Automorphisms of the upper half-plane
concepts.summary: The conformal self-maps of the upper half-plane are exactly the Möbius maps with real coefficients and positive determinant, so the automorphism group is SL2(R) modulo ±1; it is conjugate to the disc automorphisms through the Cayley transform.

concepts.name: Harmonic function
concepts.summary: A twice continuously differentiable real function on an open subset of the plane whose Laplacian u_xx + u_yy vanishes. Real and imaginary parts of holomorphic functions are harmonic, and harmonic functions are characterized by the mean-value property.

concepts.name: Harmonic conjugate
concepts.summary: For a harmonic u, a real function v with u + iv holomorphic. On a simply connected domain one exists, unique up to an additive constant, obtained from a primitive of u_x − i u_y; on other domains it may exist only locally, as log|z| on the punctured plane shows.

concepts.name: Harmonic composed with holomorphic
aliases: harmonic functions under conformal change of variables
concepts.summary: If u is harmonic and f is holomorphic with values in u's domain, then u composed with f is harmonic, with Laplacian |f'|^2 times the Laplacian of u at f; so conformal maps transport harmonic functions and boundary-value problems.

concepts.name: Mean-value property
aliases: mean value theorem for harmonic functions
concepts.summary: The value of a holomorphic or harmonic function at the centre of a closed disc inside its domain equals its average over the boundary circle, and also its average over the disc; for holomorphic functions this is the integral formula on a circle.

concepts.name: Maximum principle for harmonic functions
concepts.summary: A harmonic function on a connected open set that attains a local maximum (or minimum) is constant; on a bounded domain with continuous extension to the closure, both extremes are attained on the boundary.

concepts.name: Dirichlet problem
aliases: boundary value problem for the Laplacian
concepts.summary: Given continuous boundary data on a domain, find a harmonic function inside that extends continuously to the data. On bounded domains a solution is unique by the maximum principle; on the disc it exists and is given by the Poisson integral.

concepts.name: Mean-value property characterizes harmonicity
concepts.summary: A continuous function satisfying the circular mean-value identity on all small discs is harmonic; in particular a function that is both subharmonic and superharmonic is harmonic. Proofs compare with the harmonic solution having the same boundary values, or smooth by a radial mollifier.

concepts.name: Poisson integral formula
concepts.summary: Integrating continuous boundary values on the unit circle against the Poisson kernel (1 − |z|^2)/|e^{iθ} − z|^2 over 2π yields the harmonic function in the disc with those boundary values; the kernel is the real part of (e^{iθ} + z)/(e^{iθ} − z).

concepts.name: Harnack's inequality
concepts.summary: A nonnegative harmonic function on the disc of radius R satisfies (R − r)/(R + r) u(0) ≤ u(z) ≤ (R + r)/(R − r) u(0) for |z| = r, from two-sided bounds on the Poisson kernel.

concepts.name: Upper semicontinuous function
concepts.summary: A function into the reals extended by −∞ whose lim sup at every point is at most its value there; equivalently each set where it is below a given level is open. Such a function attains its maximum on compact sets.

concepts.name: Subharmonic function
concepts.summary: An upper semicontinuous function, possibly −∞, whose value at each point is at most its average over every small circle centred there; for twice-differentiable functions this is equivalent to a nonnegative Laplacian. Superharmonic functions are their negatives.

concepts.name: Maximum principle for subharmonic functions
concepts.summary: A subharmonic function on a connected open set that attains its maximum is constant; consequently, on a bounded domain, a subharmonic function lying below a harmonic one on the boundary lies below it inside.

concepts.name: log|f| is subharmonic
concepts.summary: For f holomorphic on an open set, log|f| (set to −∞ at the zeros) is subharmonic, and harmonic where f has no zeros; log|z| is the basic example, harmonic off the origin but not on the whole plane.

concepts.name: Jensen's formula
concepts.summary: For f holomorphic near a closed disc of radius R about 0 with f(0) ≠ 0 and no zeros on the circle, the circle average of log|f| equals log|f(0)| plus the sum over interior zeros of log(R/|a_k|), counted with multiplicity.

concepts.name: Smoothing by a radial mollifier
concepts.summary: Replacing a locally integrable function by its convolution with a smooth, compactly supported, nonnegative kernel of integral one rescaled to width ε; the result is smooth, and for functions with the mean-value property a radial kernel reproduces the function exactly.

concepts.name: Baire category theorem
concepts.summary: In a complete metric space a countable intersection of dense open sets is dense; equivalently the space is not a countable union of nowhere-dense closed sets. Used to show that generic objects, such as holomorphic functions with no analytic continuation, exist.

concepts.name: Fourier transform
concepts.summary: The transform sending an integrable function f on the real line to the function of ξ given by integrating f(x) e^{-2πixξ} over x (other conventions rescale ξ). It turns translation into modulation and convolution into multiplication, and is inverted by the conjugate kernel.

concepts.name: Gaussian integral
aliases: integral of exp(-x^T A x/2 + J^T x)
concepts.summary: For a positive-definite symmetric n x n matrix A and a vector J, the integral of exp(-x.Ax/2 + J.x) over R^n equals (2 pi)^{n/2} det(A)^{-1/2} exp(J.A^{-1}J/2); the one-dimensional case is that e^{-x^2} integrates to sqrt(pi). It is proved by squaring and polar coordinates (n = 1), then diagonalizing A and completing the square. It normalizes the normal density, and differentiating in J gives Gaussian moments as sums over pairings.

concepts.name: Ring
concepts.summary: A set with addition and multiplication such that addition forms an abelian group, multiplication is associative with an identity element, and multiplication distributes over addition. Conventions differ on whether an identity and commutativity are required.

concepts.name: Unit of a ring
concepts.summary: An element with a two-sided multiplicative inverse. The units of a ring form a group under multiplication, written R^x; for example the units of Z are 1 and -1.

concepts.name: Zero divisor
concepts.summary: A nonzero element a for which some nonzero b gives ab = 0. Rings without zero divisors allow cancellation of nonzero factors.

concepts.name: Nilpotent element
concepts.summary: An element some power of which is zero. A ring with no nonzero nilpotent elements is called reduced; every integral domain is reduced.

concepts.name: Nilradical
concepts.summary: In a commutative ring, the set of all nilpotent elements; it is an ideal and equals the intersection of all prime ideals.

concepts.name: Integral domain
concepts.summary: A nonzero commutative ring with no zero divisors, so that a product of nonzero elements is nonzero and nonzero factors can be cancelled.

concepts.name: Field
concepts.summary: A nonzero commutative ring in which every nonzero element is a unit. Every field is an integral domain, and every finite integral domain is a field.

concepts.name: Subring
concepts.summary: A subset of a ring that contains 1 and is closed under addition, negation and multiplication, hence is a ring with the inherited operations.

concepts.name: Direct product of rings
concepts.summary: The ring of pairs (r, s) with componentwise operations. Its units, ideals and prime ideals are described componentwise, and the projections to each factor are surjective ring homomorphisms.

concepts.name: Quadratic integer ring
concepts.summary: Rings of the form Z[sqrt D] for a square-free integer D: elements a + b sqrt D with a, b integers. They are the basic test cases for units, irreducibles and unique factorization.

concepts.name: Norm on a quadratic ring
concepts.summary: The map N(a + b sqrt D) = a^2 - D b^2, equal to the product of an element with its conjugate. It is multiplicative, and an element is a unit exactly when its norm is plus or minus 1.

concepts.name: Gaussian integers
concepts.summary: The ring Z[i] of complex numbers a + bi with integer coordinates. Division with remainder for the norm makes it a Euclidean domain, hence a PID and a UFD.

concepts.name: Failure of unique factorization in Z[sqrt(-5)]
concepts.summary: In Z[sqrt(-5)] the element 6 factors as 2 times 3 and as (1 + sqrt(-5))(1 - sqrt(-5)) into irreducibles that are not associates, so the ring is not a UFD; the ideal (2, 1 + sqrt(-5)) is not principal.

concepts.name: Polynomial ring
concepts.summary: Formal polynomials with coefficients in a ring, added and multiplied in the usual way. Over an integral domain, degree is additive, R[X] is again a domain, and its units are the units of R.

concepts.name: Division algorithm for polynomials
concepts.summary: If g has a unit leading coefficient, every polynomial f can be written uniquely as f = qg + r with deg r < deg g. Over a field this holds for every nonzero g.

concepts.name: Factor theorem and root bound
concepts.summary: a is a root of f exactly when (X - a) divides f. Consequently a nonzero polynomial of degree n over an integral domain has at most n roots.

concepts.name: Evaluation homomorphism
concepts.summary: For a commutative ring R and an element a, the map R[X] -> R sending f to f(a) is a ring homomorphism; its kernel consists of the multiples of X - a. More generally polynomial rings are free: a homomorphism out of R[X] is fixed by where R and X go.

concepts.name: Divisibility and associates
concepts.summary: In an integral domain, a divides b if b = ac for some c; a and b are associates if each divides the other, equivalently if they differ by a unit factor.

concepts.name: Irreducible element
concepts.summary: A nonzero non-unit that cannot be written as a product of two non-units. In a domain every prime element is irreducible, but not conversely.

concepts.name: Prime element
concepts.summary: A nonzero non-unit p such that whenever p divides a product ab it divides a or b; equivalently the principal ideal (p) is a nonzero prime ideal.

concepts.name: Greatest common divisor
concepts.summary: A common divisor of a and b that every common divisor divides; unique up to associates when it exists. In a PID it generates the ideal (a, b), so it is a linear combination of a and b.

concepts.name: Euclidean algorithm
concepts.summary: Repeated division with remainder, replacing (a, b) by (b, r) until the remainder vanishes; the last nonzero remainder is a gcd, and back-substitution writes it as a linear combination of a and b.

concepts.name: Euclidean domain
concepts.summary: An integral domain with a size function such that any element can be divided by any nonzero element leaving a remainder of smaller size (or zero). Z, polynomials over a field and the Gaussian integers are examples.

concepts.name: Unique factorization domain
concepts.summary: An integral domain in which every nonzero non-unit is a product of irreducibles, uniquely up to order and unit factors. In a UFD irreducibles are prime and gcds exist.

concepts.name: Principal ideal domain
concepts.summary: An integral domain in which every ideal is generated by a single element.

concepts.name: Euclidean domains are PIDs
concepts.summary: In a Euclidean domain any nonzero ideal is generated by one of its elements of smallest size, since the remainder of any other element on division by it lies in the ideal and is smaller.

concepts.name: Principal ideal domains are UFDs
concepts.summary: In a PID irreducible elements are prime and ascending chains of principal ideals stabilize, which together give existence and uniqueness of factorization into irreducibles.

concepts.name: Polynomial rings over a UFD are UFDs
concepts.summary: If R is a UFD then so is R[X]; the proof uses Gauss's lemma on contents of primitive polynomials and factorization over the fraction field. Hence Z[X] and k[X, Y] are UFDs.

concepts.name: Sums of two squares
concepts.summary: An odd prime is a sum of two squares exactly when it is 1 mod 4; more generally a positive integer is a sum of two squares iff primes 3 mod 4 occur to even powers. The proof factors p in the Gaussian integers.

concepts.name: Ring homomorphism
concepts.summary: A map between rings that preserves addition, multiplication and the identity. Its kernel is an ideal and its image a subring; it is injective exactly when the kernel is zero.

concepts.name: Ideal
concepts.summary: An additive subgroup of a ring that absorbs multiplication by arbitrary ring elements. Ideals are exactly the kernels of ring homomorphisms; prime and maximal ideals are special kinds.

concepts.name: Ideal generated by a set; principal ideals
concepts.summary: The smallest ideal containing a given subset: in a commutative ring, all finite linear combinations of its elements with ring coefficients. An ideal generated by one element is principal.

concepts.name: Sums, products and intersections of ideals
concepts.summary: For ideals I and J, the sum I + J is the smallest ideal containing both, I cap J the largest inside both, and the product IJ is generated by products ij; always IJ is contained in I cap J.

concepts.name: Fields have only trivial ideals
concepts.summary: A nonzero commutative ring is a field exactly when its only ideals are 0 and the whole ring; consequently every ring homomorphism from a field to a nonzero ring is injective. The zero ring is the only ring with 1 = 0.

concepts.name: Quotient ring
concepts.summary: For an ideal I, the cosets r + I form a ring with operations induced from R, and the projection R -> R/I is a surjective homomorphism with kernel I. Z/nZ is the basic example.

concepts.name: Universal property of the quotient ring
concepts.summary: A ring homomorphism from R that kills an ideal I factors uniquely through the projection R -> R/I. This is the tool for defining maps out of quotients.

concepts.name: First isomorphism theorem for rings
aliases: R/ker f is isomorphic to im f
concepts.summary: A ring homomorphism f induces an isomorphism from R/ker f onto the image of f.

concepts.name: Correspondence theorem for ideals
concepts.summary: Ideals of R/I correspond bijectively, preserving inclusion, to ideals of R containing I, via image and preimage under the projection; prime and maximal ideals correspond to prime and maximal ideals.

concepts.name: Second isomorphism theorem for rings
concepts.summary: For a subring S and an ideal I of R, S + I is a subring, S cap I is an ideal of S, and (S + I)/I is isomorphic to S/(S cap I).

concepts.name: Third isomorphism theorem for rings
concepts.summary: For ideals I contained in J, the image J/I is an ideal of R/I and (R/I)/(J/I) is isomorphic to R/J.

concepts.name: Maximal ideal
concepts.summary: A proper ideal not contained in any strictly larger proper ideal.

concepts.name: Prime ideal
concepts.summary: A proper ideal P such that ab in P forces a in P or b in P. Every maximal ideal is prime, and in Z the nonzero prime ideals are the ideals pZ.

concepts.name: Maximal ideals give field quotients
aliases: R/M is a field iff M is maximal
concepts.summary: In a commutative ring an ideal M is maximal exactly when R/M is a field, by the correspondence theorem and the ideal criterion for fields.

concepts.name: Prime ideals give domain quotients
aliases: R/P is a domain iff P is prime
concepts.summary: In a commutative ring an ideal P is prime exactly when R/P is an integral domain; hence maximal ideals are prime.

concepts.name: Existence of maximal ideals
concepts.summary: Every proper ideal of a ring (with 1) is contained in a maximal ideal; the proof applies Zorn's lemma to proper ideals ordered by inclusion, using that a union of a chain of proper ideals is proper.

concepts.name: Chinese remainder theorem
concepts.summary: If ideals I and J are coprime (I + J = R) then R/(I cap J) is isomorphic to R/I x R/J; for integers, congruences modulo coprime moduli can be solved simultaneously.

concepts.name: Ring of fractions
concepts.summary: For a multiplicative subset D of a commutative ring, formal fractions r/d with an equivalence relation that kills elements annihilated by D. It is the universal ring in which the elements of D become units.

concepts.name: Field of fractions
concepts.summary: The ring of fractions of an integral domain by all its nonzero elements; it is the smallest field containing the domain, as Q is for Z.

concepts.name: Module over a ring
concepts.summary: An abelian group with a scalar multiplication by ring elements satisfying the vector-space axioms; modules over a field are vector spaces and Z-modules are abelian groups.

concepts.name: Equivalence relation
concepts.summary: A reflexive, symmetric and transitive relation. Its equivalence classes partition the set, and every partition arises this way; quotient constructions are built from such classes.

concepts.name: Partial order
concepts.summary: A reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive relation. A chain is a totally ordered subset, an upper bound of a subset dominates all of it, and a maximal element has nothing strictly above it.

concepts.name: Zorn's lemma
concepts.summary: If every chain in a nonempty partially ordered set has an upper bound, the set has a maximal element. It is equivalent to the axiom of choice and is the standard tool for existence of maximal objects.

concepts.name: Group
concepts.summary: A set with an associative binary operation, an identity element and inverses for every element. Abelian groups are those whose operation is commutative.

concepts.name: Subgroup
concepts.summary: A nonempty subset of a group closed under the operation and under inverses; equivalently a subset that is a group with the restricted operation. Intersections of subgroups are subgroups.

concepts.name: Subgroup generated by a set
concepts.summary: The smallest subgroup containing a given subset: all finite products of its elements and their inverses. A group is generated by a set when this subgroup is everything.

concepts.name: Order of an element
concepts.summary: The least positive n with g^n = e, or infinity if there is none. g^m = e exactly when the order divides m, and the order equals the size of the cyclic subgroup generated by g.

concepts.name: Cyclic group
concepts.summary: A group generated by one element; it is isomorphic to Z or to Z/nZ. Every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic, and a cyclic group of order n has exactly one subgroup of each order dividing n.

concepts.name: Groups of prime order are cyclic
concepts.summary: A group whose order is a prime p is cyclic, generated by any non-identity element, by Lagrange's theorem; in particular it is simple and abelian.

concepts.name: Dihedral group
concepts.summary: The symmetry group of a regular n-gon, of order 2n, generated by a rotation r of order n and a reflection s with s r s = r^-1.

concepts.name: Quaternion group
concepts.summary: The non-abelian group of order 8 formed by plus or minus 1, i, j, k with i^2 = j^2 = k^2 = ijk = -1. Every subgroup is normal, and it is not isomorphic to the dihedral group of order 8.

concepts.name: Symmetric group
concepts.summary: The group of all bijections of a set to itself under composition; for an n-element set it has n! elements. Every group of permutations of a set is a subgroup of it.

concepts.name: Cycle decomposition of a permutation
concepts.summary: Every permutation of a finite set is a product of disjoint cycles, unique up to order; the cycle lengths give its cycle type, and its order is the lcm of those lengths.

concepts.name: Conjugacy classes of the symmetric group
concepts.summary: Conjugating a permutation by sigma relabels each entry of its cycles by sigma. Hence two permutations are conjugate in S_n exactly when they have the same cycle type.

concepts.name: Sign of a permutation
concepts.summary: The homomorphism from S_n to plus or minus 1 sending each transposition to -1; a permutation is even or odd according to the parity of any factorization into transpositions, and an r-cycle has sign (-1)^(r-1).

concepts.name: Alternating group
concepts.summary: The kernel of the sign homomorphism: the even permutations, a normal subgroup of index 2 in S_n for n at least 2. It is generated by 3-cycles.

concepts.name: Simplicity of A_n for n >= 5
concepts.summary: For n at least 5 the alternating group has no normal subgroups other than the trivial group and itself. A_4 is not simple, since it contains a normal Klein four-group.

concepts.name: Isometries and symmetry groups
concepts.summary: Distance-preserving maps of Euclidean space form a group; the isometries that map a figure onto itself form its symmetry group, which acts on the vertices, edges and faces of the figure.

concepts.name: Symmetry group of the cube
concepts.summary: The 48 isometries of a cube, or its 24 rotations. The rotation group acts faithfully on the four long diagonals and is isomorphic to S_4; the full group is that times the central inversion.

concepts.name: Group action
concepts.summary: A rule letting each group element act as a permutation of a set, compatibly with the group operation. It sorts the set into orbits, and each point has a stabilizer subgroup.

concepts.name: Permutation representation of an action
aliases: action as a homomorphism to Sym(X)
concepts.summary: An action of G on X is the same thing as a homomorphism G -> Sym(X); the action is faithful when this homomorphism is injective.

concepts.name: Morphism of group actions
concepts.summary: A map between two sets acted on by the same group that commutes with the actions. A bijective one identifies the two actions.

concepts.name: Orbit-stabilizer theorem
concepts.summary: For an action of G and a point x, g Stab(x) -> gx is a bijection from left cosets of the stabilizer onto the orbit; so the orbit size is the index of the stabilizer, and divides |G| when G is finite.

concepts.name: Cayley's theorem
concepts.summary: Every group is isomorphic to a subgroup of a symmetric group, via the action of the group on itself by left multiplication; a group of order n embeds in S_n.

concepts.name: Group homomorphism
concepts.summary: A map between groups that preserves the operation, so also identities and inverses. Its kernel is a normal subgroup, its image a subgroup, and it is injective exactly when the kernel is trivial.

concepts.name: Conjugation and conjugacy classes
concepts.summary: Elements g and h are conjugate if h = x g x^-1 for some x; this is the orbit relation of the action of a group on itself by conjugation. Conjugate elements have equal orders.

concepts.name: Centralizer and normalizer
concepts.summary: The centralizer of a subset consists of the elements commuting with each of its members; the normalizer of a subgroup H consists of the x with x H x^-1 = H. Both are subgroups, and the centralizer of g is the stabilizer of g under conjugation.

concepts.name: Center of a group
concepts.summary: The elements that commute with every element of the group. It is a normal abelian subgroup, and the whole group exactly when the group is abelian.

concepts.name: Automorphisms and inner automorphisms
concepts.summary: The isomorphisms of a group with itself form a group Aut(G). Conjugation by an element is an inner automorphism; these form a normal subgroup isomorphic to G modulo its center.

concepts.name: Coset and index
concepts.summary: For a subgroup H, a left coset is a translate gH. Left cosets partition the group into blocks of size |H|, and their number is the index [G : H].

concepts.name: Lagrange's theorem
concepts.summary: In a finite group, the order of a subgroup divides the order of the group, since the cosets partition it into equal pieces; hence element orders divide |G| and g^|G| = e.

concepts.name: Normal subgroup
concepts.summary: A subgroup N with g N g^-1 = N for every g, equivalently whose left and right cosets agree. Normal subgroups are exactly the kernels of homomorphisms.

concepts.name: Quotient group
concepts.summary: For a normal subgroup N, the cosets of N form a group under (aN)(bN) = abN, and the projection G -> G/N is a surjective homomorphism with kernel N.

concepts.name: First isomorphism theorem for groups
aliases: G/ker f is isomorphic to im f
concepts.summary: A homomorphism f: G -> H induces an isomorphism from G/ker f onto the image of f.

concepts.name: Product of subgroups
concepts.summary: For subgroups H and K the set HK has |H||K|/|H cap K| elements; it is a subgroup exactly when HK = KH, for instance when one of them is normal. Two normal subgroups meeting trivially commute elementwise.

concepts.name: Second (diamond) isomorphism theorem for groups
concepts.summary: If H is a subgroup and N is normal then HN is a subgroup, H cap N is normal in H, and HN/N is isomorphic to H/(H cap N).

concepts.name: Third isomorphism theorem for groups
concepts.summary: For normal subgroups N contained in M, M/N is normal in G/N and (G/N)/(M/N) is isomorphic to G/M.

concepts.name: Correspondence (lattice) theorem for groups
concepts.summary: Subgroups of G/N correspond bijectively, preserving inclusion, index and normality, to subgroups of G containing N.

concepts.name: Lattice of subgroups
concepts.summary: The subgroups of a group ordered by inclusion, drawn as a diagram with joins (generated subgroups) and meets (intersections); a compact way to record a small group's structure.

concepts.name: Simple group
concepts.summary: A nontrivial group whose only normal subgroups are the trivial subgroup and itself. Cyclic groups of prime order are the abelian simple groups.

concepts.name: Composition series
concepts.summary: A chain of subgroups from the trivial group up to G, each normal in the next, with every successive quotient simple. Every finite group has one.

concepts.name: Jordan-Holder theorem
concepts.summary: Any two composition series of a finite group have the same length and the same composition factors up to order and isomorphism.

concepts.name: Solvable group
concepts.summary: A group with a chain of subgroups from the trivial group to G, each normal in the next, with abelian quotients; for finite groups, one whose composition factors all have prime order.

concepts.name: Class equation
concepts.summary: For a finite group, |G| equals |Z(G)| plus the sum of the indices of the centralizers of representatives of the non-central conjugacy classes.

concepts.name: p-group
concepts.summary: A finite group whose order is a power of a prime p. A nontrivial p-group has nontrivial center, by the class equation; groups of order p^2 are abelian.

concepts.name: Cauchy's theorem for finite groups
concepts.summary: If a prime p divides the order of a finite group, the group has an element of order p.

concepts.name: Sylow theorems
concepts.summary: For a finite group of order p^a m with p not dividing m: subgroups of order p^a exist, they are all conjugate, and their number is 1 mod p and divides m.

concepts.name: Classification of groups of small order
concepts.summary: Determining all groups of a given small order up to isomorphism by combining Lagrange, Cauchy, Sylow counting, the class equation and direct products.

concepts.name: Minkowski metric
concepts.summary: The symmetric bilinear form diag(1,-1,-1,-1) (mostly-minus convention) on four-dimensional spacetime; it defines the invariant interval t^2 - x^2 and is used to raise and lower spacetime indices.

concepts.name: Lorentz group
concepts.summary: The group of real 4x4 matrices Lambda with Lambda^T eta Lambda = eta, i.e. the linear maps preserving the Minkowski metric. It contains rotations and boosts; its identity component excludes parity and time reversal.

concepts.name: Lorentz algebra
concepts.summary: The Lie algebra of the Lorentz group: six generators (three rotations J_i, three boosts K_i), or antisymmetric M^{mu nu}, fixed by their commutation relations. Near the identity a Lorentz matrix is 1 + omega with omega_{mu nu} antisymmetric.

concepts.name: Representations of the Lorentz group
concepts.summary: An assignment of matrices to Lorentz transformations that respects composition, describing how field components mix: trivially for scalars, by Lambda for four-vectors and by one Lambda per index for tensors, while the spacetime argument is transformed separately.

concepts.name: Spinor representations
concepts.summary: The two-component complex representations of the Lorentz algebra built from Pauli matrices, on which a 2 pi rotation acts as -1; they are genuine representations of the double cover SL(2,C). A Dirac spinor is the direct sum of a left- and a right-handed Weyl spinor.

concepts.name: Projective representation
concepts.summary: A map from a group to operators that respects multiplication only up to a phase factor. Because quantum states are rays, symmetries need only act projectively; the projective representations of the Lorentz group are the representations of its double cover.

concepts.name: Clifford algebra of gamma matrices
concepts.summary: Four matrices gamma^mu whose anticommutators equal twice the metric; any solution yields a four-dimensional spinor representation of the Lorentz algebra. Explicit choices (Dirac, Weyl or Majorana bases) are related by change of basis.

concepts.name: Spinor Lorentz generators
concepts.summary: The matrices built from commutators of gamma matrices satisfy the Lorentz-algebra commutation relations, so their exponentials give the action of Lorentz transformations on four-component spinors; gamma^mu then transforms as a four-vector under this action.

concepts.name: Dirac equation
concepts.summary: The first-order, Lorentz-covariant wave equation for a four-component spinor field, obtained as the Euler-Lagrange equation of the Lagrangian psi-bar (i gamma^mu partial_mu - m) psi; each component also satisfies the Klein-Gordon equation.

concepts.name: Majorana fermion
concepts.summary: A spinor field built from a single Weyl spinor that is its own conjugate; a Lorentz-invariant mass term can be written with one Weyl spinor and the antisymmetric sigma_2 pairing, unlike a Dirac mass, which pairs a left- with a right-handed spinor.

concepts.name: Lorentz invariance
concepts.summary: The requirement that the laws of a theory take the same form in every inertial frame, so that actions and amplitudes are built from Lorentz scalars. Many long-wavelength systems realize it emergently with an effective speed of light.

concepts.name: Four-vectors and tensor index notation
concepts.summary: Spacetime vectors carry an upper index and covectors a lower one; repeated upper-lower pairs are summed and the metric converts one into the other. Derivatives with respect to symmetric tensor components need a symmetrized identity.

concepts.name: Lorentz-invariant one-particle measure
concepts.summary: The measure d^3p / ((2 pi)^3 2E_p) on the positive-energy mass shell. It equals d^4p restricted by delta(p^2 - m^2) times the step function in p^0, which shows it is invariant under orthochronous Lorentz transformations.

concepts.name: Mass shell and on-shell condition
concepts.summary: The hyperboloid p^2 = m^2 with positive energy in momentum space. Free particles and plane-wave solutions of the free wave equation are on shell; internal lines of a covariant perturbation expansion carry off-shell momenta.

concepts.name: Scalar field
concepts.summary: A real or complex function on spacetime whose value at a physical point is the same in every frame; under a Lorentz transformation the field is relabelled, phi'(x') = phi(x), without mixing components.

concepts.name: Klein-Gordon equation
concepts.summary: The linear second-order equation (box + m^2) phi = 0 for a free scalar field. Its plane-wave solutions satisfy the relativistic dispersion relation, and it is the Euler-Lagrange equation of the free scalar Lagrangian.

concepts.name: Action principle
concepts.summary: Classical field configurations make the action, the spacetime integral of the Lagrangian density, stationary under variations that vanish at the boundary; total derivatives in the Lagrangian can be dropped because they only contribute boundary terms.

concepts.name: Lagrangian density
concepts.summary: A local function of fields and their first derivatives whose spacetime integral is the action. Terms bilinear in fields are kinetic or mass terms; terms with three or more fields are interactions.

concepts.name: Euler-Lagrange equations
aliases: equations of motion from a Lagrangian
concepts.summary: The equations of motion partial_mu (dL/d(partial_mu phi)) - dL/dphi = 0, one per field, obtained by requiring the action to be stationary and integrating by parts.

concepts.name: Small fluctuations about a classical vacuum
aliases: mass from the second derivative of the potential
concepts.summary: Expanding a field about a constant solution at a minimum of the potential and keeping linear terms gives a free wave equation for the fluctuation, whose squared mass is the curvature of the potential at that minimum.

concepts.name: Spontaneous symmetry breaking
concepts.summary: A symmetry of the dynamics fails to fix a chosen ground state. The symmetry group maps that vacuum to a family of degenerate vacua, and the subgroup fixing it is the unbroken symmetry group.

concepts.name: Global symmetry
